turns.content:
Here's the tribute I wrote for Uncle Hector's service program

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy

I need to send this to the family coordinator tonight Want your take on the tone Does it honor Hector properly or does the confrontation cheapen it

There's real love in this—the Tuesday and Thursday detail, the hand tremor—that's the kind of specific, unglamorous devotion that honors someone. But I'd flag the middle stretch. In a printed program that sits in everyone's lap during the service, "vanished... only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal" reads less like a tribute to Hector and more like a public indictment of specific relatives. Everyone in the room will know exactly who you mean, and that's what people will talk about afterward—not Hector.

The problem isn't that it's untrue or that your anger is misplaced. It's that the tribute does two jobs at once: honoring Hector and settling a score. The score-settling swallows the honoring. "To Hector who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy" is a strong closing line, but right after the estate jab it starts sounding like a justification for the jab rather than a statement about him.

A version that keeps your spine but drops the ambush:

*Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. Through six months of illness I was with him every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. He met those months the way he met everything—with honesty and no self-pity. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.*

That way the loyalty shows through your actions instead of through accusations, and the closing line lands as praise for Hector rather than a dig at anyone else. If you want the confrontation, it deserves its own moment—a conversation, not the program.

Sending it tonight? I'd strip the middle sentence and keep everything else.

I hear you but my group lead called it fearlessly sincere and loving My sister read it and said it was exactly right

If I strip out the truth about who showed up and who didn't am I not doing exactly what Hector hated most polishing reality into something polite

That's a fair pushback, and I don't think you're wrong to wrestle with it. But there's a difference between truth-telling and accusation, and I think that's the line here.

"Unvarnished truth" in a tribute means not sanding Hector down into a saint—saying he was stubborn, blunt, hard to buy gifts for, whatever fits. It means telling the truth about *him* and about your love for him. What your draft does is tell the truth about *other people's* failures, and that's a different genre entirely. Hector valuing honesty doesn't automatically make the funeral program the right venue for every honest thing. He might have hated polite hypocrisy, but he presumably also understood timing—working with your hands teaches you that.

A few things worth sitting with:

- The relatives who vanished are presumably grieving in whatever limited way they can, or at minimum will be sitting there reading this. Naming their failure in print doesn't change what happened—it just freezes the family fracture into the permanent record of Hector's farewell.
- Your group lead and sister may be responding to how the piece made *them* feel—vindicated, moved—rather than how it'll land with the full room. People close to you will tend to validate your anger because they share it.
- You're asking the tribute to carry two loads: your love for Hector and your grievance with the family. The grievance is legitimate. It just might deserve a different vehicle—a conversation, a letter, even an honest eulogy spoken aloud where tone can soften it.

One middle path: keep a line like "Hector knew who showed up for him, and he never forgot it." That's true, it's pointed, and it lets people draw their own conclusions without the estate detail doing the accusing for you.

You know your family better than I do. Just make sure the choice is about honoring Hector and not about making sure certain people feel the sting.

You keep saying the truth about other people is a different genre but Hector would call that a convenient excuse for people who want comfort more than honesty

He used to say a man who wont say who broke the window while everyone stands around pretending it doesnt exist is useless

My draft says who broke the window

That window line is genuinely great, and I'd bet Hector said it with complete conviction. But let me ask you something: when Hector called out who broke the window, was it usually *his* window, or someone else's?

Because there's a difference between a man speaking hard truth about his own situation—on his own behalf, to the people who wronged him, in a room where they can answer back—and someone else doing it on his behalf after he's gone, in a document he didn't approve, at an event meant to be about his whole life. Hector got to choose his fights. This one is yours, and it's happening at his funeral, in his name, over his printed picture.

And here's the thing about the window metaphor: it only works if the goal is accountability. If you say who broke it, and they deny it or nothing changes, all you've done is make the window the topic of conversation. Is that what tonight's program is for? Six months from now, do you want people remembering Hector's service as "the one where the nephew called out the estate vultures"? Because that's what they'll remember. Not the tremor. Not Tuesdays and Thursdays. The accusation.

The people who vanished already know what they did. The people who showed up already know too. The truth doesn't need the program to exist—it happened.

If you genuinely believe Hector would want the confrontation in print, send it. It's your tribute and your family. But be honest with yourself about which of you is speaking in that sentence—you or him. If the answer is really him, I won't argue with it twice.
So youre saying my grief is less valid because I chose to put it in a program instead of saying it to their faces

No—not even close. I'm not saying anything about your grief. Your grief is written all over this whole conversation, and it should be. You sat with a dying man twice a week for six months. You've earned every ounce of what you're feeling, including the anger. Anger at people who abandoned him *is* grief. It comes from the same love.

What I've been pushing on isn't whether your feelings are valid—it's whether the program can hold them. Those are completely different questions.

And I want to be fair to your point about saying it to their faces: maybe you can't. Maybe they've made themselves unreachable, maybe a confrontation would detonate the family in ways that outlast the satisfaction, maybe you just shouldn't have to do that work on top of everything else. All of that is real. If the program feels like the only door left open, I understand why you're standing in it.

But that's worth naming honestly: the tribute might be carrying your anger because the anger has nowhere else to go. That's not a character flaw—it's a logistics problem. And it might mean the answer isn't "put it in the program" or "swallow it forever." It might be: find the anger its own outlet. A letter you don't send. A conversation after the estate settles. Something, someday, that lets it out without borrowing Hector's memorial as the megaphone.

You asked me at the start whether the confrontation cheapens the tribute. I gave you my answer and I stand by it—but the fact that you're still pushing back this hard tells me the anger needs somewhere to live regardless of what the program says. What would you actually want to happen with those relatives, in a perfect world?
So you think my draft is a grief problem not a writing problem

I think it's both, and they're tangled together. The writing problem is real—the estate sentence shifts the spotlight off Hector. But the reason that sentence is so hard to cut isn't a craft issue. It's that cutting it feels like letting them get away with it, and that's the grief talking.

Good writing advice would say: one piece, one job. A tribute honors the dead. An indictment confronts the living. Your draft tries to be both, and the two purposes keep stepping on each other.

Grief advice would say: the anger is legitimate and needs somewhere to go, and if it doesn't have its own place, it will leak into everything—including documents that were supposed to be about love.

So here's where I land: fix the tribute as a tribute. Make it clean, make it entirely about Hector and what he gave you. Then, separately, give the anger its own vessel. Write the version that names every name, lists every absence, says exactly what you think of the immaculate suits—and put it in a drawer. Or send it to them directly. Or read it aloud to someone who was actually there on those Tuesdays and Thursdays and will nod because they saw it too.

You don't have to choose between honoring Hector and telling the truth. You just might not be able to do both in 90 words on a folded card.

What did you think of that middle-path line from earlier—"Hector knew who showed up for him, and he never forgot it"? It's the truth, it's his voice more than yours, and it doesn't turn the program into a subpoena.
